passage: In the playground in Lagos, Ada, five, wanted to tell the teacher about her lost tooth. "It... um... I was..." She stopped and licked her lips. Yosef, the teacher, waited, looking at her with a smile. "The... tooth... it fell in... my... rice." Her words came slowly. Yosef didn't finish her sentence. She giggled, "I put it in a cup!" He said, "Thank you for waiting for the words. That's a great story." Ada beamed.

qa.q: Where did Ada's tooth fall?
qa.a: It fell in her rice.

qa.q: What might Ada have been feeling as she stopped and licked her lips?
qa.a: She might have been shy or searching for the right words. She may also have been unsure how the teacher would respond.

qa.q: What worked in the way Yosef handled Ada's slow speech?
qa.a: He waited calmly with a smile and did not finish her sentences, so Ada could say it herself.

qa.q: How might Yosef feel as he waits for Ada's words?
qa.a: He may feel patient and interested, since he kept smiling at her and did not finish her sentence.

grounding: A child's hesitant speech can be shyness or word-searching, and waiting calmly works better than finishing sentences.

passage: In the waiting area of the vaccination clinic in Chandigarh, Rafiq, six, was asked by the nurse Vinita what he liked to do at school. "I... um... I like... the... um..." He looked at his father. Vinita smiled and didn't speak. "...the... clay," he said finally. "I made a... snake." "A clay snake! Tell me more," said Vinita. Rafiq's father was about to help, but Vinita gave him a small nod. Rafiq told her about the snake's long tail.

qa.q: What did Rafiq make at school?
qa.a: He made a snake out of clay.

qa.q: What might Rafiq have been thinking as he paused and looked at his father?
qa.a: He may have been unsure about talking to a stranger, or searching for the word. He looked at his father, which suggests he wanted reassurance.

qa.q: How did Vinita help Rafiq talk?
qa.a: She waited without speaking, gave his father a small nod so he would not jump in, and asked him to tell her more.

qa.q: How might Rafiq's father feel watching him struggle?
qa.a: He may feel the urge to help, and Vinita's nod shows him it's better to wait.

grounding: A child's halting speech may be shyness or word-searching, and waiting works better than finishing his sentences.

passage: I'm Darshan, Tarun's cousin. Yesterday Tarun was telling Nani about the zoo. “We saw… a… um… the big… the… the grey one with the…” He waved his arm like a trunk. I wanted to shout “Elephant!” but his mother put a hand on my arm and just waited, looking at Tarun. Nani waited too. Tarun frowned, then said, “Elephant! And it sprayed water!” He went on and on after that. I'm not sure if he was shy or just finding the word, but waiting worked.

qa.q: What animal was Tarun trying to name?
qa.a: The elephant.

qa.q: What might Tarun have been feeling as he searched for the word?
qa.a: He may have felt a bit frustrated or shy while searching for the word. When he found it, he seemed excited to keep talking.

qa.q: Why was waiting better than finishing the sentence for Tarun?
qa.a: It let him find the word himself, which gave him confidence to keep telling the story.

qa.q: How did waiting feel for Darshan?
qa.a: It was hard for Darshan, who wanted to shout the answer, until it was clear that waiting worked.

grounding: A cousin observes a child's halting speech and sees that waiting calmly works better than finishing his sentences.

passage:
Monday: Jomon started, “Miss, my… my…” and Indu Miss said quickly, “Your pencil? Your bag? Your tiffin?” Jomon shook his head and stopped talking.
Wednesday: Jomon started, “Miss, I… I want…” Indu Miss knelt and waited, not saying a word. Jomon breathed. “I want to sit… near the window.” She nodded. “Sure.”
Friday: Jomon told her a whole story about his cat, stopping and starting, and she listened, waiting at every pause. At the end he smiled. “That's all.”

qa.q: Where did Jomon want to sit on Wednesday?
qa.a: Near the window.

qa.q: What was Jomon feeling when he shook his head and stopped talking on Monday?
qa.a: He was probably frustrated and discouraged that Indu Miss guessed wrong, so he gave up.

qa.q: What changed on Wednesday that helped Jomon?
qa.a: Indu Miss knelt and waited silently instead of guessing, giving him time to find his words.

qa.q: How might Indu Miss feel on Friday listening to the cat story?
qa.a: She probably feels pleased and glad she learned to wait, since Jomon now shares whole stories.

grounding: Over a week, a teacher learns that waiting calmly helps a child with halting speech more than finishing his sentences.

passage: The bus was crowded and noisy, and their stop was coming. Jeevan tugged Sachin Mama's kurta. “Mama… my… my slipper… it… the…” He looked at the floor. Sachin wanted to hurry; the conductor was already shouting the stop name. But he crouched and waited. Jeevan swallowed. “It fell… under the seat… when the man sat.” Sachin reached under the seat and found it. “Thank you for telling me all of it.” They jumped off just as the bus pulled away.

qa.q: Where did Jeevan's slipper fall?
qa.a: Under the seat, when the man sat.

qa.q: What was Jeevan feeling as he spoke in bits and looked at the floor?
qa.a: He was probably worried about losing his slipper and a bit shy or unsure how to explain in the noisy bus.

qa.q: Which choice by Sachin Mama worked, and why?
qa.a: He crouched and waited instead of rushing or guessing, which let Jeevan explain and the slipper was found in time.

qa.q: What would change if Sachin had hurried Jeevan off the bus?
qa.a: Jeevan might have been left without his slipper and felt that his words didn't matter.

grounding: Even under time pressure on a bus, an uncle waits calmly for a child's halting explanation instead of finishing it.

passage:
On the first day back at the city school, Lalremsiami Miss asked, "Nitin, what did you do in the holidays?"

"We... we went to the... the um..." Nitin looked at the ceiling.

"The zoo!" shouted the boy next to him.

Nitin shook his head and went quiet, looking at his shoes.

Lalremsiami Miss held up a hand to the other boy and waited, smiling, saying nothing.

"The... fish place," Nitin said at last. "Big glass. There was a... a turtle. It swam over my head."

"Over your head! Tell us more."

qa.q: What swam over Nitin's head?
qa.a: A turtle.

qa.q: What was Nitin probably feeling when he went quiet and looked at his shoes?
qa.a: He was likely frustrated and a bit discouraged after the other boy guessed wrong for him. His halting start suggests he was searching for the word, and may also have felt shy speaking to the class.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami Miss do that helped?
qa.a: She stopped the other boy from answering, waited calmly and smiled, which gave Nitin time to find his own words.

qa.q: How might the boy who shouted "The zoo!" see his guess?
qa.a: He probably thought he was helping, without noticing that finishing the sentence made Nitin stop talking.

grounding: It shows a child speaking in a halting way while searching for a word, and calm waiting working better than finishing his sentence for him.
